formationLabel: Lithuanian Roman Catholic parish established in 1908 · Rogers Street church phase documented from 1911 · exact terminal instrument unresolved
currentUse: The Lithuanian St. Joseph parish is historical. The Archdiocese of Boston identifies it as a Lithuanian ethnic parish established in 1908, distinct from Lowell's French Saint Jean Baptiste/Saint Joseph lineage. A later field survey identifies the former church at 151 Rogers Street and reports conversion to apartments after parish closure. That survey supports a converted-building reading, but no canonical closure decree, exact effective terminal date, current property record, or records-custody notice has been located.
summary: St. Joseph was Lowell's Lithuanian Roman Catholic parish, established in 1908 according to the Archdiocese of Boston. It is not the French Saint Jean Baptiste/Saint Joseph parish established in Lowell in 1868. Local and field histories describe an early hosted phase associated with a Polish St. Casimir church, followed by a Lithuanian church at 151 Rogers Street in 1911. A field survey reports that the parish closed in 2003 and the church was converted to apartments, but the exact canonical terminal act and effective date remain unresolved.

historicalNarrative.text: Lowell contained more than one Catholic institution using the St. Joseph name. The Archdiocese of Boston lists Saint Jean Baptiste/Saint Joseph as a French parish established in 1868 and separately lists Lithuanian St. Joseph as an ethnic parish established in 1908. The two lineages are distinct and are not joined by their shared saint name or city.

historicalNarrative.text: The Archdiocese dates the Lithuanian parish to 1908. The Lowell Historical Society timeline gives 1909 and says the Lithuanian community had previously used a Polish St. Casimir church. Without the canonical erection instrument, the one-year difference remains unresolved and may reflect different organizing and establishment milestones.

Field documentation identifies the Lithuanian parish church at 151 Rogers Street and dates its construction to 1911. The exact address of the earlier Polish host church and the duration of hosted worship remain unresolved, so the host is recorded separately and is not assigned the Rogers Street site identity.

The field survey reports that St. Joseph closed in 2003 and that its Rogers Street church was converted to apartments. No archdiocesan decree or official closure notice has been located, so 2003 remains an attributed terminal reading rather than a fully resolved canonical date. The reported conversion concerns the building and does not itself identify the parish's terminal mechanism.

The converted-building reading rests on field documentation rather than a current property or occupancy record. The former church's present ownership, apartment configuration, interior condition, and the location of sacramental records remain unresolved. No cemetery or successor-parish relationship is asserted without direct evidence.
